leads.title: As India's Weakest Monsoon in Over a Decade Hits Maharashtra, One Village Shows What Relief Work Can Build
leads.summary: According to its sarpanch, Popatrao Pawar, around 90% of the residents of Hiware Bazar, a village in Maharashtra's Ahilyanagar district (earlier Ahmednagar), had migrated by the early 1990s, and only 13% of its farmland could be irrigated.  The village lies in a rain shadow and receives about 400 mm of rain a year. Down To Earth reported in 2017 that its crop production did not fall in 2015, when it received around 50% less rain than normal. That record carries fresh relevance. India's monsoon ended 12.6% below average, its weakest in more than a decade, a senior India Meteorological Department official told Reuters on 30 September, 2026. Maharashtra recorded an 18% deficit and declared 265 of its 358 tehsils drought-affected on 26 September, 2026. A rulebook from 1880 Paying people to build public assets during drought is an old idea. The Famine Commission of 1880 recommended Famine Codes to guide officials in anticipating and relieving crop failure.  According to economist Jean Drèze, their backbone was public works paying subsistence wages within reach of workers' homes, supported by early warning, with specific guidelines on how to recognise and declare a famine.    Hiware Bazar used drought relief funds to build contour trenches and water-harvesting structures, restoring farmland and bringing migrant families home.   After Independence, the codes became Scarcity Manuals, and during the 1972-73 drought in Maharashtra, as many as 5 million people attended relief works at the peak of distress. Public works remain part of the response. Maharashtra has earmarked Rs 6,728 crore under its rural employment mission , and the number of households seeking Employment Guarantee Scheme work rose from 402,493 in July to 493,169 in September. leads.title: 1 Million Children, 57 Years: How Mobile Creches is Building a Childcare Infrastructure for Working Parents
leads.summary: This article has been published in partnership with Mobile Creches. By 8 am, the first children are walking into the creche at Aashiyana, a construction site in Gurugram where their parents work. Lalita is already there. "We look at every child from head to toe," she says. "Then we talk to the parents. What did the child eat last night? How did they sleep? Is anything troubling them?" It is a small ritual, repeated for 48 children every morning. For mothers who hand their children over and walk back into a day of work, it matters most. "A mother going to work may not know everything the child learns here," Lalita says. "What she knows is that one didi is taking care of her child and she can work in peace."   At a construction site in Gurugram, parents begin their workday while their children head to the Mobile Creches centre, where care worker Lalita is ready to welcome them.   Lalita, 32, has been that didi (elder sister/care giver) for nearly 12 years, a milestone she completes this November. As India marks the UN Global Day for Care and Support on 29 October, and Mobile Creches hosts its India Childcare Champions Awards a day earlier, her story asks a bigger question: what does it take to care for a country's youngest children well, and who should share the load? The teacher who stayed At 20, Lalita, then a private school teacher, noticed a Mobile Creches training centre near her home in South Delhi. "I felt strongly that yes, I should work here," she says. She now runs Aashiyana and its bridge course.
